summary.one_liner: sd is a command-line find-and-replace tool that uses familiar regex syntax by default, with a string-literal mode and in-place file editing.
summary.what_it_does: sd takes a search pattern and a replacement string as separate arguments and applies them to stdin or to files. By default it treats patterns as regular expressions using JavaScript/Python-style syntax. The -F/--fixed-strings flag switches to literal matching. Capture groups can be referenced by index ($1) or by name (named groups like (?P<name>...)), and $$ escapes a literal dollar sign. Files are modified in place, and -p previews changes. By default it processes input line by line to keep memory low and stream output; the -A/--across flag allows patterns to match across line boundaries, such as replacing newlines. The README includes benchmarks against sed showing it is faster on large JSON files and simple replacements.
use_cases: replace text across many files in a project
find and replace in a file in place
replace literal strings containing regex special characters
swap or reformat captured groups in text
notable: Regex syntax familiar from JavaScript and Python instead of sed/awk quirks
Literal string mode via -F with no escaping needed
Line-by-line processing by default with low memory use and streaming stdin output
Across mode (-A) for multi-line patterns like matching newlines
Named and indexed capture groups in replacement strings
caveats: Line-by-line default means patterns cannot span lines unless -A is used, which uses more memory (about 74 MB peak in the README benchmark versus 3 MB)
Arguments starting with '-' are parsed as flags, so they need a -- separator
